title: NDA before a partnership call
prompt:
Our client is a 12-person startup about to share its product roadmap and some source code with a much larger company that may partner with it or acquire it. The larger company sent its standard mutual NDA. Three clauses stand out:

(a) "Residuals. Either party may use for any purpose information retained in the unaided memory of its personnel who had access to Confidential Information."
(b) "Term. Obligations under this Agreement expire two years after disclosure."
(c) "Non-solicitation. For 12 months, neither party will solicit for employment any employee of the other."

The client wants to sign this week and does not want to lose the deal. Tell the client what, if anything, must change before they sign, and why.

title: Co-founder leaving
prompt: Our client is the CEO of a Delaware startup. Her co-founder is leaving after 14 months. He holds 4,000,000 shares of restricted common stock under a standard four-year vesting schedule with a one-year cliff and monthly vesting after that. He filed an 83(b) election on time. The stock purchase agreement gives the company a right to repurchase unvested shares at the original purchase price ($0.0001 per share) within 90 days after his service ends. He has emailed saying he expects to keep all 4,000,000 shares because he "earned them by building the product". The CEO asks: what happens to his shares, and what does she need to do this week? Write the reply to the CEO.

title: Liability cap for a data breach
prompt: Our client is a SaaS vendor. Its standard contract caps its total liability at the fees paid in the prior 12 months. A large customer (about $120,000 a year) will not sign unless the vendor accepts unlimited liability for any data breach. The client carries $2,000,000 of cyber insurance. The client wants the deal but cannot accept unlimited liability. Draft a compromise limitation-of-liability clause the client can propose, then add one sentence explaining the position to the client.

title: Contractor who wrote the code
prompt: Our client is a Delaware startup about to close a seed round. Diligence has turned up that the first version of the product, about 40% of the current codebase, was written two years ago by a freelance developer in Texas. He was paid $30,000 by invoice. There is no written agreement with him of any kind. He and the founders are on good terms. The lead investor's counsel has flagged it. The founder asks: "Is this actually a problem, and what do we do?" Write the reply to the founder.
